King Charles discussed slavery during his opening speech of the Commonwealth summit, held in Antigua and Barbuda. In his address to the gathered presidents and prime ministers, Charles spoke about slavery with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow".
The King told Commonwealth leaders the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow", but did not offer an apology. Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to "address the wrongs of the past with action for the future".
Burnham announced that he is, unlike any other prime minister before him, willing to start discussions about a formal apology from the British state for its role in slavery. Burnham appeared to rule out reparations: "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part".
